title: 16 Indians Killed in Middle East Since February, Government Tells Parliament
excerpt: India disclosed that ten merchant seafarers and six other nationals have died in the escalating US-Iran conflict, underscoring the risks facing over 300,000 Indian sailors worldwide.
body:
• Sixteen Indian nationals, including ten merchant seafarers, have been killed in the Middle East since February as a result of the escalating US-Iran conflict, India's government disclosed in Parliament on Wednesday.
  • Three Indian crew members died aboard the tanker Settebello, which was struck during military operations in the Gulf of Oman in March.
  • India summoned both U.S. and Iranian diplomats after the attacks to demand accountability for civilian casualties affecting its nationals.
  • Over 300,000 Indian sailors serve on commercial vessels worldwide, making the merchant fleet one of the country's most exposed diaspora populations in conflict zones.

Parliament Reveals the Full Toll

India's External Affairs Ministry disclosed on Wednesday that 16 Indian nationals have been killed in the Middle East since February, a figure that lays bare the rising human cost of the US-Iran conflict for one of the world's largest diaspora populations. The disclosure came in response to a parliamentary question and represents the first time New Delhi has provided a comprehensive accounting of Indian casualties in the escalating hostilities.

https://x.com/PTI_News/status/2083033372087992573

Of the 16 dead, ten were merchant seafarers killed while serving on commercial vessels caught in or near conflict zones in the Persian Gulf, the Gulf of Oman, and the Red Sea. The remaining six were Indian workers and professionals based in countries across the broader Middle East.

The Settebello Attack

The deadliest single incident involved the oil tanker Settebello, which was struck during military operations in the Gulf of Oman in March. Three Indian crew members were killed in the attack. India's government lodged strong protests with both the United States and Iran following the incident, summoning diplomats from both countries to demand answers and accountability.

"India has consistently maintained that the safety and security of Indian nationals abroad, including our seafarers, is a matter of the highest priority."

— Ministry of External Affairs spokesperson

The broader pattern of attacks on commercial shipping in the region has affected dozens of vessels since late 2024, driven primarily by Houthi militia strikes in the Red Sea and retaliatory US military operations near Iran's coastline.

A Vulnerable Workforce

India supplies one of the largest contingents of merchant sailors in the world. Over 300,000 Indian seafarers serve on international commercial vessels, accounting for roughly 12% of the global merchant fleet workforce. These sailors operate on oil tankers, container ships, and bulk carriers that transit some of the world's most dangerous waterways, including the Strait of Hormuz and the Bab el-Mandeb strait.

The families of many of these seafarers hail from coastal states including Maharashtra, Kerala, Gujarat, and Tamil Nadu. Merchant shipping remains a critical source of foreign remittances and middle-class employment, particularly for communities in smaller port cities.

India's Diplomatic Tightrope

The casualties underscore the diplomatic tightrope New Delhi walks in the Middle East. India maintains close economic and energy ties with both the United States and Iran, and has sought to avoid being drawn into the conflict. It imports significant quantities of oil from the Gulf states and has strategic port investments in Iran's Chabahar.

At the same time, the Modi government faces growing domestic pressure to do more to protect Indian workers and sailors in the region. Opposition members in Parliament pressed for details on what concrete steps had been taken to secure safe passage for Indian-crewed vessels.

What's Next

India's shipping ministry has issued updated advisories urging Indian-crewed vessels to avoid designated high-risk zones and maintain communication with naval coordination centers. The Indian Navy has maintained a presence in the Arabian Sea and Gulf of Aden as part of anti-piracy patrols, but the scale of the current threat from state and militia actors goes well beyond what naval escorts alone can address.

For the families of the 16 dead, the parliamentary disclosure was a grim confirmation of losses that had largely gone unacknowledged in the national media. Maritime unions have called for enhanced insurance coverage and hazard compensation for sailors deployed to conflict-affected routes.
